Donating Customer-Returned Merchandise

Bottom Line Up Front

Donate returned and unsold goods through a nonprofit, transfer them as-is with indemnification, and screen out recalled and regulated items — and legal liability is very low. For food and grocery, which is the bulk of a supermarket's divertible inventory, federal law provides broad immunity and no donor has ever been held liable in a reported case.

Liability by Product Category

Category
Governing Protection
Risk
Food — perishable & shelf-stable
Bill Emerson Act + Food Donation Improvement Act (2022): federal civil & criminal immunity.

Same Emerson Act protection — it covers "grocery products" (paper, cleaning, detergents, household), not only food.

Rx/OTC drugs, cosmetics, medical devices, infant/children's items, any recalled product: special rules — some can't be redistributed at all.

*General-merchandise risk is low when the program runs through a nonprofit, transfers goods as-is, and includes indemnification.

The Protections, in Brief

The Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act (42 U.S.C. § 1791), strengthened in 2022, shields both the donor and the nonprofit distributor from civil and criminal liability for the condition of donated food and grocery products, and raises the bar so a donor is only liable for gross negligence or intentional misconduct. General merchandise sits outside that act, but a free donation made through a nonprofit also sits outside the commercial "stream of commerce" where product liability normally attaches — and as-is transfer plus indemnification closes the rest of the gap.

Keep Liability Low — and What to Exclude

Do this — every category
Donate through a registered 501(c)(3).
Transfer as-is, with a written no-warranty disclaimer.
Donation agreement with hold-harmless + indemnification.
Keep records: receipts, condition notes, recall-screen attestation.
Screen out / exclude
Any recalled item — illegal to donate (CPSA § 19).
Prescription & OTC drugs, cosmetics, medical devices.
Infant/children's items needing CPSIA testing (cribs, car seats).
Anything known to be defective or unsafe.

Informational only, not legal advice. Laws vary by state and product type; the donating company should have its own counsel review any donation program and agreements before implementation.
